# Dispatch Control Center v1

**For:** Mike Zachary, Owner/Operator, Level 1 Transport
**Generated by:** Claude Code · 2026-08-24

You do not need a terminal and you do not need to type a Python command.
**Double-click `dispatch.bat` in the Dispatch folder.** That is the whole thing.

A window opens showing the current status, then eight controls:

```
  [1] ▶ Start
  [2] 🌐 Open Dispatch
  [3] 🔄 Refresh Status
  [4] ⚙ Settings
  [5] ℹ Version
  [6] ↻ Restart
  [7] ⎌ Reset Session
  [8] ■ Stop Dispatch
  [Q] Quit
```

Type the number and press Enter. You can also type the word — `start`, `stop`,
`settings` — if that is faster than looking for the number.

**If the icons do not appear, nothing is wrong.** A Windows console that has not
been switched to UTF-8 cannot draw them, so the Control Center leaves them out
rather than printing garbage or crashing. The numbers are what you type either
way.

---

## The eight controls

**▶ Start** — starts one Dispatch server and records which process it is. If
Dispatch is already running it tells you so and starts nothing; you cannot end up
with two by pressing this twice. If it will not start, you get a sentence you can
act on — *"Dispatch could not start because port 8080 is already in use"* — and
the technical detail goes to the log.

**🌐 Open Dispatch** — opens the portal in your browser. If the browser cannot be
opened for you, the address is printed to type in yourself. If Dispatch is not
running, it says so rather than opening a page that will not load.

**🔄 Refresh Status** — takes a new reading of everything below. Creates nothing,
changes nothing.

**⚙ Settings** — every setting Dispatch consults, whether it is set, what it is
for, what happens without it, and **the exact command to change it**. Secrets are
listed by name and their values are never shown, here or in any log. The Control
Center does not store settings of its own: Dispatch reads them from Windows
environment variables and this screen reads the same ones, so there is never a
second answer to "what is Dispatch actually using".

**ℹ Version** — the Dispatch version, the **commit** (which is what actually
proves which code is running — quote it when reporting anything), your Python
version and interpreter, and the packages Dispatch depends on.

**↻ Restart** — stops the running server, proves it is gone, and only then starts
a new one. The new process ID will differ from the old one; if it does not,
something is wrong and the screen will say so.

**⎌ Reset Session** — clears the Control Center's own leftover state so the next
Start begins clean. Specifically: a stale process record (the thing that makes a
launcher insist Dispatch is running on a machine where it is not), an old failure
message that has already been dealt with, and a rehearsal binding left set in
this window.

> **Reset Session never deletes freight.** No load, milestone, driver, truck,
> evidence file, POD or database record is touched, and there is no flag that
> makes it so. It also **refuses while Dispatch is running** — clearing the
> record of a live server is exactly how you end up with an orphan that still
> holds the port and can no longer be stopped from here. Stop first, then reset.
>
> Purging rehearsal *data* is a different thing entirely, it is your decision,
> and it lives in `scripts/dispatch_proof.py purge-plan`, which reports what
> would be removed and deletes nothing.

**■ Stop Dispatch** — stops the server and confirms the process is actually gone
rather than assuming it. If it did not exit, you are told, and told what to do.
Stop is deliberately the last item: it is the one control you must not hit by
reaching for a neighbour.

---

## What the status screen shows

Every line is read from this machine at the moment you look at it. Nothing on it
is a default standing in for something that was not read — where a value could
not be established it says `UNCONFIGURED`, `UNAVAILABLE` or `UNVERIFIED`, and
means it.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Status** | `RUNNING` with the process ID, or `STOPPED`. Plus a warning if something is answering on the port that this Control Center did not start. |
| **Version** | Dispatch's version, and the commit. |
| **Portal URL** | The address Dispatch would actually use, including the loopback pinning that development mode applies. |
| **Database Path** | The `dispatch.db` file in use. |
| **Operations Path** | `DISPATCH_OPERATIONS_ROOT`, or `UNCONFIGURED - using defaults`. |
| **Archive Path** | Where archives go — and, if nobody set it, marked `(default - DISPATCH_ARCHIVE_ROOT is not set)`. |
| **Memory Path** | The same, for evidence and the library. |

It also shows the mode (operational or development), whether a missing security
setting is stopping Dispatch from starting (**by name, never by value**), the
last backup and where it is, the log directory, and the most recent start
failure in plain language.

**On backups, one thing worth knowing:** the screen will not call a backup
*valid*. It tells you when one was taken and where it is, and it says
`UNVERIFIED` until a restore has actually been proven into a separate empty
folder. An unverified backup is a hope, and you will find out which at the worst
possible moment.

---

## This is a control, not a second Dispatch

The Control Center starts, stops and observes the Dispatch you already have. It
holds no freight data, has no database of its own, and duplicates none of the
portal's functionality. It cannot create, change or delete a load, a milestone,
a driver or an evidence file — not because it is careful, but because it has no
code path that could: it never imports the modules that own operational data,
and a test in the repository fails the build if that ever changes.

Everything it displays it reads through Dispatch's own resolvers, in a separate
process, so it cannot drift into reporting a database location or a port that
the portal does not actually use.

---

## If something goes wrong

**"Dispatch is already running" but nothing is running.** A stale process record.
Use **⎌ Reset Session**.

**"Something is already answering on port 8080, but this launcher did not start
it."** An orphan from a previous crash, or another program on the port. The
screen names the process ID when Windows will tell it. Close that process, or
change `PORTAL_PORT` in **⚙ Settings**.

**"Dispatch will refuse to start until this is set."** A security setting is
missing. **⚙ Settings** names it and prints the `setx` command. Remember that
`setx` only reaches windows opened *afterwards* — close this one and reopen it.

**A red `REHEARSAL MODE` banner in the portal.** Dispatch is in rehearsal and
every record it creates is tagged `REHEARSAL`. That is correct during a
rehearsal and wrong during real work. **⎌ Reset Session** clears the binding for
this window.

**Anything else.** The log directory is on the status screen. Secrets are
redacted before anything is written there.

---

## Not yet proven on your machine

Everything above is `UNVERIFIED` until you run it on Windows. The Control Center
has been exercised end to end on Linux — start, double-start refusal, HTTP
reachability, restart with the old process confirmed dead, stop, and secret
redaction in the logs — but that is evidence of software behaviour, not
operational proof. `proof/launcher/LAUNCHER_PROOF.md` lists all eight acceptance
items with the exact command for each and a blank column for what you observe.

Six things only your machine can answer: whether `py.exe` is installed and points
at the interpreter that has Flask; whether PowerShell will run
`Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` for your account; whether `taskkill` is
permitted; whether the `D:` environment variables reach a double-clicked `.bat`;
whether Defender or SmartScreen interferes with a detached process; and whether
your console renders the status block correctly.
